osintX.content:
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said it disabled the Palau flagged bulk carrier M/V Pacific Archer in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday, Nov. 26th, after the crew "attempted to run" the U.S. blockade following departure from Bandar Abbas, Iran.

AIS data from MarineTraffic shows the vessel was on course to exit the Gulf of Oman late Nov. 24th or early Nov. 25th when it turned sharply north and ran nearly parallel to the blockade line at 12.8 knots. At 0815 UTC it slowed to 0.6 knots, and at 1316 UTC it turned back into the Gulf of Oman at 5 to 6 knots.

At 2000 UTC on Nov. 25th (0000 local time on Nov. 26th), the vessel was about 70 nautical miles from the blockade line, heading into the Gulf of Oman at 4.9 knots. It continued toward the anchorage off Fujairah, United Arab Emirates (UAE), throughout Nov. 26th.

The data appears difficult to reconcile with CENTCOM's description of an attempt to run the blockade on Nov. 26th and appears to indicate that the strike was conducted as the vessel was transiting away from the blockade line. AIS is self reported and can be manipulated, however this vessel's track does not appear to show indicators of being spoofed.

osintX.content:
Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's Cloud One, its cloud computing platform, according to a report from Reuters. The intrusion was discovered within the past month or so during a system upgrade and has disrupted the platform. 

Cloud One hosts applications that manage Air Force personnel data, pay, logistics and maintenance, along with systems that track air defense radar feeds and munitions. 

Sources said migration of back office applications has been paused, updates to existing applications were blocked, and some users lost administrator rights. One source said the intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the platform's control plane, which could in theory give access to operational data such as aircraft status, though it is unclear whether they did. Cyber Command has been called in to assess the damage. The Air Force declined to comment on specific networks.

Before NVIDIA’s Board of Directors announced earlier this week that it would be reinstating Jensen Huang as President and CEO, appearing to be at the behest of President Trump and others at the White House; the Pentagon and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth were weighing the use of the 1950 Defense Production Act to force NVIDIA to restore Huang, three people familiar with the debate have told The Washington Post.

Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, discussed how the DPA could be used as leverage to pressure NVIDIA’s Board of Directors to restore an executive to a company that they argued was critical to the national security of the United States. 

While the law provided no clear path to installing Huang back as CEO, it could be used as a warning. “Essentially they could use the DPA to force NVIDIA to shift more of its production to military projects,” said one of the three people, a member of the Trump Administration. Potentially curbing future production plans and profits of NVIDIA.
